notes:
I found commentary on all five verses, but not much on the second and third parts of your request. Most of what I found is older commentary and one Church Father (Augustine). On v. 3 the commentators disagree over which Hebrew reading is correct, but they don't split along denominational lines. I found nothing from Pentecostal, Lutheran, Orthodox or prosperity / word-of-faith / hyper-grace teachers, and no NET Bible or bibleodyssey notes, so those are left out.

---

**Title / overview**

- Guzik says this is the only psalm in the collection with the title "A Psalm of Thanksgiving." He reads it as an invitation to the whole earth to know and worship God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-100/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes "There is not a single mournful note in the composition." It says the psalm must be read alongside Psalms 93 and 95–99. That whole series both celebrates and predicts Jehovah coming to rule the whole world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-100.html
- The Expositor's Bible calls it the end of the "Psalms of the King." The call to praise comes twice, each time followed by reasons: first God's dealings with Israel (v. 3), then His character as shown in all His works (v. 5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/100.htm
- **Catholic:** Augustine's Latin and Greek Bibles titled it "A Psalm of confession," and he takes the title as a cue to ask what "jubilating with confession" means. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801100.htm. The Greek and Latin text on New Advent's Bible page (where the psalm is numbered 99) reads "Psalmus in confessione." https://www.newadvent.org/bible/psa099.htm

**v. 1**

- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says it is a call to the nations, reaching far beyond Israel's borders. He quotes Spurgeon: the word means the glad shout loyal subjects give when their king appears, and "Our happy God should be worshipped by a happy people." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-100/
- Matthew Henry: the summons will be fully answered when all nations are discipled and the gospel is preached to every creature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_100.cfm
- **Catholic:** Augustine explains "jubilate" as a wordless sound of joy, a mind pouring itself out in gladness. He compares it to reapers and grape-harvesters shouting as they work. He warns against jubilating with the voice while the heart does not. He links the "all lands" call to the Church spreading from Jerusalem to all nations. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801100.htm

**v. 2**

- **Traditional reading:** Guzik thinks the psalmist probably meant temple worship, but says the principle covers any service done for God, and it should be done gladly. He says singing is not the only way to praise God, but it is the chief way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-100/
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** it is our privilege and duty to be happy in worship. Anyone the religion of Christ has not made happy either misunderstands it or is misusing it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-100.html
- The Pulpit Commentary's homilies point to the elder brother in the prodigal parable as a servant with no joy. They say this is why Paul rejoices that we are under grace, not law: only then is real service given. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-100.html
- **Catholic:** Augustine says this service holds no bitterness, because it is a sweet service and we are all redeemed. The believer is both slave (as a creature) and free (as one loved by God). Elsewhere he says to serve in "the gladness of love" and lets the conscience rejoice, not just the tongue. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801100.htm ; https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.C.html

**v. 3**

- **Traditional reading:** Guzik gives three reasons to worship here: He is God, He is Creator, and He has chosen a people and shepherds them. For Christians there is a greater reason still: they are a new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-100/
- Matthew Henry: God made us, so we are not our own but His. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/100-3.html
- **The main textual question ("not we ourselves" or "we are His"):** In Hebrew, "not" and "his" sound the same (*lô*) but are spelled differently.
  - The Cambridge Bible prefers "we are His": it adds a new thought rather than a simple contrast, and it fits the Hebrew sentence and parallels such as Psalm 95:7.
  - The Pulpit Commentary prefers the KJV's "not we ourselves." It notes the Greek and Latin versions and the old commentators back it, and says it should be kept because it gives the better sense.
  - Barnes judges that the weight of authority favours "and not we," meaning we did not create ourselves.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/100-3.htm
- **Different readings across traditions:**
  - **Reformed (Calvin):** "His people… sheep of His pasture" means the distinguishing grace by which God set apart His children as His own, a far greater privilege than simply being born human. Calvin keeps "not we ourselves" but says the other reading does not change the meaning. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_100_1-3.htm
  - **Geneva Bible notes:** "made us" mainly means spiritual regeneration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/100-3.htm
  - **Baptist (John Gill):** we did not make ourselves, either as creatures or as new creatures. Regeneration is solely the Lord's work. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/psalms/100-3.html
  - **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** he rejects "not we ourselves," asking whether any people, however pagan, ever believed they made themselves. He prefers "His we are," found in 26 Hebrew manuscripts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/100-3.html
  - **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** whichever reading is right, the thought is accurate, whether or not it is justified in the text. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/100-3.html
  
  These are differences in emphasis (election, regeneration, or the textual question) rather than outright doctrinal clashes.
- **Catholic:**
  - Augustine reads "Know that the LORD is God" as aimed at the crucified Christ: the One they scourged and crucified is God. He links "He made us" to John 1:3. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.C.html
  - The Knox translation on New Advent follows the "His we are" reading: "his we are, he it was that made us". https://www.newadvent.org/bible/psa099.htm

**v. 4**

- **Traditional reading:** Guzik pictures worshippers from all lands entering the temple gates and courts, and stresses corporate worship. He quotes Boice: some thanksgiving involves the whole people of God together, not just private prayer. Under the New Covenant even the way into the Holy of Holies is open (Hebrews 10:19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-100/
- Spurgeon's *Treasury* quotes Francis Hill Tucker: the gates of His church are open even to the most guilty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps100.cfm
- Matthew Henry: praise must run like a golden thread through every duty (Hebrews 13:15), in every ordinance as well as every providence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_100.cfm

**v. 5**

- **Traditional reading:** Guzik quotes Boice: unlike the selfish, unpredictable pagan gods, "The God of the Bible is and has always been good." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-100/
- The Pulpit Commentary: "truth" means His faithfulness, keeping the word or promise He has spoken. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-100.html
- The Cambridge Bible notes that "Give thanks… for He is good; His lovingkindness endures forever" became a standing liturgical formula after the exile. Barnes grounds praise in God's character: His kindness, His mercy, and His truth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/100-5.htm
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** mercy and compassion are forms of God's goodness. Because His nature is eternal, His mercy must be everlasting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-100.html
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** toward His own people mercy has been theirs from all eternity, and shall be theirs world without end. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps100.cfm
- **Baptist (Gill):** he reads the verse in terms of Christ, the good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/100-5.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** the more we praise God, the stronger we grow, and the sweeter He becomes. His mercy does not stop once He has freed us; it protects us all the way to eternal life. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.C.html
